title: Hot and Sour Soup (Suān Là Tāng)
description: Hot and Sour Soup is a classic Chinese soup known for its bold contrast of sourness, peppery heat, savory broth, tender mushrooms, bamboo shoots, tofu, and delicate egg ribbons. A rich clear stock combined with Chinkiang black vinegar and white pepper creates the characteristic balanced flavor, while cornstarch gives the soup a silky restaurant-style texture.

ingredients.title: For the Broth Base
items: High-quality chicken stock – 6 cups, unsalted, clear, and rich
Dried shiitake mushrooms – 3, rehydrated in hot water, stems removed and thinly sliced
Wood ear mushrooms – ½ cup, rehydrated and thinly sliced
Firm tofu – 100 g, cut into thin strips
Lean pork tenderloin or chicken breast – 100 g, julienned

ingredients.title: For the Aromatics & Seasoning
items: White pepper – ½ tsp, freshly ground, plus more to taste
Chinese black vinegar – 3 tbsp (Chinkiang preferred, adjusted to taste)

instruction.title: Step 1 – Preparing the Protein
steps: Place the julienned pork or chicken in a bowl.
Lightly marinate with 1 tsp soy sauce, ½ tsp cornstarch, and ½ tsp Shaoxing wine.
Mix well and set aside while preparing the broth.

instruction.title: Step 2 – Building the Broth
steps: Pour the chicken stock into a large wok or soup pot and bring it to a gentle simmer.
Add the rehydrated shiitake mushrooms, wood ear mushrooms, bamboo shoots, and tofu.
Simmer gently for approximately 5 minutes to allow the flavors to develop.

instruction.title: Step 3 – Cooking the Protein
steps: Add the marinated pork or chicken strips to the simmering broth.
Stir gently to separate the strips.
Cook for 2–3 minutes, or until the protein is just cooked through.

instruction.title: Step 4 – Seasoning the Soup
steps: Add light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, white pepper, and ground Sichuan pepper if using.
Add the Chinese black vinegar and stir thoroughly.
Taste the soup and adjust the vinegar and white pepper until it has a bold sour flavor with a pronounced peppery kick.

instruction.title: Step 5 – Thickening the Broth
steps: In a small bowl, mix the cornstarch with cold water until completely smooth.
Stir the slurry again immediately before adding it to the soup.
Slowly drizzle the slurry into the simmering broth while stirring continuously.
Cook briefly until the soup becomes glossy and lightly thickened.

instruction.title: Step 6 – Creating the Egg Ribbons
steps: Reduce the heat to low and create a gentle circular swirl in the soup.
Slowly drizzle the beaten eggs into the moving broth in a thin, steady stream.
Continue stirring gently in one direction to form delicate egg ribbons.
Avoid vigorous stirring, which can break the eggs into small flakes.

instruction.title: Step 7 – Final Touch
steps: Stir in the sesame oil just before removing the soup from the heat.
Taste once more and adjust the vinegar or white pepper if necessary.

instruction.title: Step 8 – Garnishing & Serving
steps: Ladle the hot soup into warmed serving bowls.
Top with finely sliced green onions and fresh cilantro if using.
Serve immediately with additional black vinegar or chili oil on the side if desired.

servingSuggestions.title: Serving Suggestions
items: Serve hot as an appetizer before a Chinese meal.
Offer extra Chinkiang black vinegar or chili oil at the table for guests to adjust the flavor.
Pair with fried rice, noodles, dumplings, or other Chinese dishes.
For a vegetarian version, replace chicken stock and meat with vegetable stock and additional tofu or mushrooms.

chefTips: Use a rich, clear stock for the best foundation; chicken bones simmered with ginger and scallions can produce an excellent homemade stock.
Adjust sourness primarily with black vinegar and heat primarily with white pepper for a traditional flavor profile.
The finished soup should be glossy and silky rather than overly thick; add cornstarch slurry gradually to control the consistency.
Stir the cornstarch slurry immediately before adding because it settles quickly.
For delicate egg ribbons, keep the soup at a gentle simmer and stir slowly in one direction while adding the beaten egg.
Add sesame oil at the very end so its fragrance remains fresh.
For a vegetarian or vegan version, use vegetable stock, omit the pork or chicken, and replace the egg with additional tofu or another plant-based protein.
